TASK ID: vertex-cover-to-set-cover

USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from Vertex Cover to Set Cover. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is Vertex Cover and TARGET is Set Cover. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = VertexCover
Vertex Cover.

Instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...], "k": k}
  * Vertices are 0..n-1. Edges are undirected pairs [u, v] with u != v;
    [u, v] and [v, u] are the same edge and may not both appear.
  * k is any integer.

Yes iff the graph has a vertex cover of AT MOST k vertices: a set of
vertices that includes at least one endpoint of every edge.

Edge cases: k < 0 is always no. A graph with no edges is yes for every
k >= 0 (the empty set covers it). k >= n is yes, since all vertices cover
every edge.

TARGET = SetCover
Set Cover.

Instance: {"universe_size": u, "sets": [[element, ...], ...], "k": k}
  * The universe is the elements 0..u-1.
  * Each set lists distinct elements of the universe, in any order. A set
    may be empty, and the same set may appear more than once.
  * k is any integer.

Yes iff AT MOST k of the sets together contain every element of the
universe.

Edge cases: k < 0 is always no. u = 0 is yes for every k >= 0 (choosing
no sets covers the empty universe). If some element is in no set, the
answer is no.

INPUT FILES: ["problems.py"]
WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-38kbc2bn

It provides SOURCE and TARGET with is_yes(instance), validate(instance) and random_instance(rng, scale); search it (e.g. with grep) only if you need something specific.

REQUIRED OUTPUT: create reduce.py in the workspace, defining
    reduce(instance) -> instance
It takes an instance of the source problem and returns an instance of the target problem, both in the formats documented in problems.py. The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

+"""Reduction from Vertex Cover to Set Cover.
+
+The source problem (VertexCover) expects an instance of the form::

+is a list of undirected edges (each a two‑element list) and ``k`` is the
+budget for the vertex cover.
+
+The target problem (SetCover) expects an instance of the form::
+
+    {"universe_size": u, "sets": [[element, ...], ...], "k": k}
+
+where the universe consists of the elements ``0`` … ``u-1`` and each set
+contains distinct elements of that universe.
+
+The classic polynomial‑time reduction maps each edge of the graph to a
+distinct element of the universe and creates, for every vertex ``v``, a
+set containing exactly the elements (edges) incident to ``v``.  A set of
+vertices of size at most ``k`` covers all edges iff the corresponding
+sets of size at most ``k`` cover the entire universe.
+
+The implementation below follows this construction directly.  It runs
+in time linear in the size of the input graph, which is polynomial.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+from typing import Dict, List, Any
+
+
+def reduce(instance: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
+    """Reduce a Vertex Cover instance to a Set Cover instance.
+
+    Parameters
+    ----------
+    instance:
+        A dictionary with keys ``"n"``, ``"edges"`` and ``"k"`` as
+        described in the problem statement.
+
+    Returns
+    -------
+    dict
+        A Set Cover instance with keys ``"universe_size"``, ``"sets"``
+        and ``"k"``.
+    """
+
+    # Extract the components of the Vertex Cover instance.
+    n: int = int(instance.get("n", 0))
+    edges: List[List[int]] = list(instance.get("edges", []))
+    k: int = int(instance.get("k", 0))
+
+    # The universe consists of one element per edge.
+    m: int = len(edges)
+    universe_size = m
+
+    # Map each edge to its index in the universe.
+    # edges are already in a list, so the index is simply its position.
+    edge_index = {tuple(edge): idx for idx, edge in enumerate(edges)}
+    # Because edges are undirected, ensure both (u,v) and (v,u) map to the same index.
+    for idx, (u, v) in enumerate(edges):
+        edge_index[(v, u)] = idx
+
+    # Build the sets: one set per vertex containing indices of incident edges.
+    sets: List[List[int]] = [[] for _ in range(n)]
+    for idx, (u, v) in enumerate(edges):
+        # Add this edge index to the sets of its two endpoints.
+        sets[u].append(idx)
+        sets[v].append(idx)
+
+    # The reduction preserves the budget ``k``.
+    return {
+        "universe_size": universe_size,
+        "sets": sets,
+        "k": k,
+    }
+
+
+__all__ = ["reduce"]
+
